claims.text: Increasing local chemical short-range order in single-phase high-entropy alloys raises lattice friction.
Chemical short-range order modifies dislocation interactions and slip behavior.
Greater short-range order systematically increases hardness and strength relative to more random atomic distributions.
The controlled comparison should use single-phase FCC CrCoNi-based alloys with uniform grain size and identical thermal history.
Systematically varying Cr, Co, and Ni ratios can control the extent and character of short-range order.
Using identical processing will hold grain size and annealing-related effects fixed while composition is varied.
Nanoscale chemical clusters or ordered regions occur in the CrCoNi matrix.
The extent and distribution of nanoscale ordered regions alter dislocation glide.
Localized chemical ordering produces compositional fluctuations or chemical heterogeneities.
Ordering-induced compositional fluctuations increase the energy barrier to dislocation motion.
The increased barrier to dislocation motion elevates both strength and hardness.
Alloys with more pronounced short-range order will have at least 10–20% higher hardness than otherwise similar alloys without significant short-range order.
Alloys with more pronounced short-range order will have at least 10–20% higher strength than otherwise similar alloys without significant short-range order.
Rapid quenching or suitable composition selection can produce a fully randomized HEA with minimal short-range order.
The proposed SRO-hardening relationship primarily applies to near-equimolar, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys with measurable short-range order.
BCC, multiphase, or negligible-SRO alloys may not exhibit the predicted hardening effect.
Electron nanodiffraction can reveal short-range order in CrCoNi.
Atom probe tomography can be used to characterize local chemical heterogeneity associated with short-range order.
The magnitude of SRO-associated changes in hardness and strength may vary among alloy systems and processing routes.
A failure of SRO variation to correlate with a 10–20% increase in hardness and strength, or a failure to alter dislocation behavior, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The comparison is said to use identical thermal histories and heat treatments, but one proposed route for producing the randomized baseline is rapid quenching, which would introduce a different thermal history and potentially different defect and microstructural states.

The intervention changes elemental composition to tune SRO, while the predicted comparison is described as between otherwise chemically similar specimens. Composition itself can affect phase constitution and mechanical properties, so the proposed comparison does not cleanly isolate SRO.
